name: Pharma and AI Biotech Partnerships
blurb: How drugmakers buy AI discovery: collaborations, milestones and royalties.
title: Pharma and AI Biotech Partnerships
answer: Most large drugmakers access AI discovery through partnerships with AI biotechs rather than building everything in house. Typical deals pay a modest upfront sum and much larger milestone payments tied to candidates reaching the clinic and market, so most headline values depend on future success.

reading.body:
Headline deal values in AI drug discovery are mostly contingent, so the upfront payment and the number of programmes are the better signals of belief.

The structure is consistent across these partnerships. A drugmaker supplies biology, data, development capacity and money. An AI biotech supplies models and specialised teams. The money splits into a modest upfront sum, research funding, milestone payments tied to candidates reaching the clinic and market, and royalties on sales. Because headline figures sum every possible milestone, they describe a best case rather than cash paid.

This matters for AI specifically because the compute and the models sit on the biotech side while the expensive, slow validation sits on the drugmaker side. A partnership is how a model gets tested against real biology without either party funding the whole pipeline. The Lilly and NVIDIA co-innovation lab is the clearest case in the data of the compute layer entering directly, pairing Lilly's biology with NVIDIA's compute rather than buying discovery from a smaller platform company.

The terms that decide the outcome are the least visible ones. Who owns the data generated in a collaboration, and whether the AI partner can reuse it to improve its models for other customers, are contract questions rather than scientific ones. The data covers deal shapes and two 2026 announcements, and it does not give upfront amounts, milestone totals, or success rates, so it cannot tell you which of these partnerships worked.

The upfront payment is the only part of a headline deal value that the drugmaker has committed regardless of outcome, which makes it the closest thing to a price the market puts on the platform. Milestones convert that price into a bet on clinical events the AI partner does not control, since the candidate still has to clear trials run by the drugmaker. The number of programmes does separate work: a single-target collaboration signals a test, while several programmes signal the drugmaker is buying the platform rather than one molecule.

The Lilly and NVIDIA lab is structurally different from the biotech collaborations in the data. In a typical deal the drugmaker buys discovery output from a company whose models it cannot inspect, while here the compute layer is contributed directly by a partner whose business is compute. That places the two scarce inputs, biology and compute, inside one arrangement and leaves the model-building to the parties themselves rather than to an outside platform.

The Iambic and Takeda collaboration shows the more common shape, where an AI platform is pointed at named disease areas in oncology, gastrointestinal and inflammation. The data records the announcement and the target areas but not the financial terms, so it cannot be used to compare the size of that deal against any other.

How should I read a deal worth billions?
Look at the upfront payment and the number of programmes. Most of the headline value is contingent on success.

Who owns data from a collaboration?
It depends on the contract, and it is one of the most important terms to negotiate.

What upfront payments have these partnerships actually paid?
The data does not hold any upfront amounts, milestone totals, or royalty rates for the deals it lists.

Which partnership in the data put compute directly into the drugmaker?
The Lilly and NVIDIA co-innovation lab, announced in January 2026, pairs Lilly's biology with NVIDIA's compute.

What disease areas did the Iambic and Takeda collaboration cover?
Oncology, gastrointestinal and inflammation targets, applied to small molecule programmes.

Have any of these partnerships produced a drug that reached the market?
The data does not say, and it gives no success rates for any of the collaborations listed.

explainer:
Most AI drug discovery reaches big pharma through partnerships. A drugmaker brings biology, data, development capacity and money; an AI biotech brings models and specialised teams. Deals usually combine a modest upfront payment, research funding, milestone payments when candidates reach defined stages, and royalties on sales. Headline values add up every possible milestone, so they describe a best case rather than money paid.

Partnerships take several forms: discovery collaborations on specific targets, platform licences, joint labs, and co-development deals that share costs and rewards. Big technology companies have also become partners, providing compute and models. The terms that matter most are often less visible, such as who owns the data generated and whether the AI partner can use it to improve its models for other customers.

How the partnerships are structured

Almost every large pharmaceutical company has signed discovery deals with AI focused biotechs, and the structures follow a few patterns. A target based deal gives the AI company a list of targets and pays milestones as candidates advance. A platform deal gives the pharma company access to the AI company's technology for its own programmes. An equity investment buys influence and a window on the technology. And acquisitions bring the capability in house. Upfront payments are usually modest; the headline figures in announcements are mostly milestones that may never be paid.

What the pharma company gets and gives

The pharma company gets speed and a method it does not have, without building a data science organisation from scratch. It gives data, targets, chemistry and the ability to run trials, which the AI company lacks. The tension is over credit and control: who owns the molecules, who decides which to advance, and whether the AI company's platform improves from the pharma company's data, which the AI company then uses with others.

What the record shows so far

Many deals have produced candidates, several have reached the clinic, and a few have reported positive trial results, but the industry is still waiting for the first approved medicine that an AI company can claim to have designed end to end. Deals have also been quietly ended when programmes stalled. The reasonable reading is that AI discovery is now a standard part of the toolkit, that the partnerships are how most companies access it, and that the proof of value will come from trial results over the next several years rather than from the deal announcements.
